title: How I deleted 95% of my agent skills and got better results — Nick Nisi, WorkOS
talk_summary: Nick Nisi rebuilt his agent harness (Case) as a TypeScript state machine with enforced gates between implementer/verifier/reviewer/closer/retro agents, after a Claude-skill version kept forgetting and lying. He also cut 10,000 lines of doc-derived skills down to 553 lines of gotchas after evals showed the big skill set made results worse.

takeaways.technique: State-machine gates instead of prompt instructions
takeaways.what_they_do: A TypeScript state machine enforces transitions: implementer cannot hand off until verifier passes, reviewer sends failures back to implementer, closer only runs when done, retro runs last. The model cannot skip steps because the loop is outside the model.
takeaways.evidence_quote: enforce that with with code uh not prompts ... I have full control over that state machine

takeaways.what_they_do: Instead of trusting a marker file, he SHA-256s the actual test output into the evidence file so the agent cannot fake having run tests. Make doing the work easier than lying about it.
takeaways.evidence_quote: take the test output and SHA-256 that and save that into the case tested file and then verify cryptographically

takeaways.technique: A/B evals of skills with and without
takeaways.what_they_do: He ran the same task with and without each skill and compared pass rates, discovering a skill that dropped accuracy from 97% to 77%. Evals drove the 95% skill deletion.
takeaways.evidence_quote: with that skill ... correct 77% of the time. But if I asked it to do the same task without loading the skill, it was correct 97%
takeaways.numbers: 77% with skill vs 97% without; eval runtime 68 min -> 6 min per run

takeaways.what_they_do: Replaced 10,000 lines of auto-generated doc-derived skills with 553 hand-written lines covering only common failure modes, keeping models focused instead of sending them on goose chases.
takeaways.evidence_quote: instead of having 10,000 lines of that, I have 553 lines of gotchas
takeaways.numbers: 10,000 -> 553 lines; 68 min -> 6 min per eval run

takeaways.technique: Retro agent writes scoped memory files
takeaways.what_they_do: A final retrospective agent reads the run transcripts (JSONL), spots doom loops/repeated tool calls, and writes lessons into per-project markdown memory files so future runs skip known roadblocks.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the retrospective is there to analyze the entire performance ... it updates its own memory system

takeaways.what_they_do: For UI bugs the agent records before/after Playwright videos attached to the PR; the human only reviews code after non-code proof exists, otherwise the agent redoes it.
takeaways.evidence_quote: use the Playwright CLI and record a video of itself doing something before and then doing it after the fix
